body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Hevy comes from its App Store listing, its help center and website, and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

If you're comparing Hevy with something else, you probably already know it's good: a quick, free workout log with a social feed, rated 4.9 stars from about 104,000 US App Store ratings. Only 15 of its 500 most recent US reviews are three stars or lower.

So this isn't a "switch now" post. If you lift from routines you wrote yourself and just want to log them, Hevy's free plan is hard to beat. Kiron (that's us) is for the many people whose training doesn't fit that: a plan that came from a coach, a book or ChatGPT, runs alongside the lifting, and weeks that don't go to plan.

Hevy or Kiron: the verdict

  • Stay on Hevy's free plan if you write your own routines and just want to log them. It logs unlimited workouts, with no ads.
  • Upgrade to Hevy Pro ($23.99 a year, or $74.99 once) if you want unlimited routines, your full history, or Hevy Trainer, which builds a lifting program and tells you when to add weight.
  • Stay with Hevy for what Kiron doesn't have: a social feed with gym leaderboards, and Apple Watch and Wear OS apps.
  • Switch to Kiron if your plan already exists somewhere else (ChatGPT, a coach, a PDF, a book), if you run as well as lift, or if you want short days, other gyms and missed days handled for you, with recovery that counts your other apps' workouts.

Bottom line: if Hevy's free plan covers what you do, keep it. Kiron is a paid app, and it earns that when your plan comes from elsewhere, includes runs, or keeps getting knocked off schedule.

Is Hevy's free plan enough?

For a lot of people, yes. The free plan logs unlimited workouts with no ads. It shows last session's weights and reps as you go, handles supersets, drop sets, warm-up and failure sets, RPE and rest timers, and lets you follow friends and save routines from Hevy's library or other lifters. According to Hevy's help center, here's where it stops:

  • 4 routines. A routine is one saved workout, so a four-day split fits and a five-day split doesn't.
  • 7 custom exercises, for anything that isn't in Hevy's library.
  • 3 months of data history. Pro keeps all of it.
  • 150 sets per workout or routine. This cap applies on Pro too, and Hevy says most workouts never come close.

Pro lifts the routine and custom-exercise limits, keeps your full history, adds set counts per muscle group and a warm-up calculator, and includes Hevy Trainer. It costs $23.99 a year, $74.99 once for life, or $2.99 to $3.99 a month (the App Store lists both monthly prices).

A 3-star reviewer in November summed up where the free plan pinches: "Adding in new workouts after the first 4 make you pay." That review is one of only 15 at three stars or lower among Hevy's 500 most recent.

Hevy Pro can now build your program

If you last looked at Hevy a while ago, this part is new: Hevy Pro includes Hevy Trainer. You answer questions about your goal, experience, equipment, how often and how long you want to train, whether to add cardio and which muscle group to prioritize, and it generates a program: workouts, exercises, rep ranges, rest periods and starting weights. As you log, it tells you when to add weight and by how much.

Hevy says Trainer's programs come from an algorithm grounded in training research, not from AI. Its July and October 2026 updates added exercise swaps (for one session or for good), injury management and more split types.

So if what you want is an app that writes your lifting program and progresses it, Hevy Pro does that for $23.99 a year. Kiron's case isn't that Hevy can't plan. It's about plans that already exist somewhere else, and weeks that hold more than lifting.

Three situations where a log isn't the whole job

1. Your plan came from somewhere else

A coach sent you a 12-week program. ChatGPT wrote you one. It's in a PDF, or a book. To follow it in Hevy, you type it in as routines, one per distinct workout. The free plan holds four, so a five-day split, or a plan whose workouts change by phase, means paying for Pro or retyping as you go. Exercise names are the other snag: a 3-star reviewer in November said their trainer's terms aren't in Hevy's library, so anything missing becomes the nearest match or one of your 7 custom exercises.

Hevy's other route is its ChatGPT app, which replaced the HevyGPT in our guide to tracking a ChatGPT workout plan. Type @hevy in ChatGPT and it can build a plan and save it to your Hevy account. It's tied to ChatGPT, though, and Hevy's routines aren't dated (its help center describes a routine as a saved workout you can do any time), so which workout falls on which day is still yours to track.

In Kiron, tap Add a program, then Import a plan, and paste the text or take a photo (or choose several, for a plan that runs across pages). Kiron reads the days, exercises, sets, reps and rest, lets you check each exercise match and edit anything before saving, then puts the plan on your calendar on the days you pick, phases in order. It doesn't open PDFs or spreadsheets, so copy the text or take screenshots.

2. You also run

Hevy is built around lifting. It logs cardio with time and distance, and Trainer can add cardio to a program, but we didn't find running plans in Hevy: nothing that builds you toward a 5K or a half marathon alongside your lifting.

Kiron puts runs, rides, swims and rows on the same calendar as your lifting, with time and distance. Its programs run from Beginner 5K to Marathon, plus Sprint Triathlon, Cycling Base and Run + Lift, and you can follow a running program and a lifting program side by side. You can shorten or lengthen a run on the day, like a lift (races stay as planned). One gap: Kiron doesn't show running pace. For spacing the two, see running and lifting in the same week.

3. The week doesn't go to plan

In Hevy, you can change a workout as you go (add or remove exercises and sets) and, with Trainer, swap an exercise for one session or for good. Routines aren't dated, so a missed day just means starting the next one when you're back. That's simple, and for many people it's enough.

In Kiron the plan lives on a calendar, so those days get their own tools. Open a workout and tap Adjust today's workout:

  • Change the duration. Fit it into less time and Kiron drops extras, pairs accessories into supersets and trims accessory sets, keeping the main lifts. Stretch it and it adds sets where your week is behind.
  • Different equipment today, or one tap for a saved gym like a hotel or a garage: Kiron swaps anything that needs gear you don't have.
  • Add to today: core, arms, shoulders, glutes, calves, a cardio finisher or stretching.

Each change is for today only, with Undo. Missed workouts show on Today with Move to a day, Pick a day or Skip; miss several and you get Push plan back, Pick days or Skip them. The recovery map counts runs, rides and ski days that other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect, so if today's session leans on legs a weekend ride already worked, Kiron says why and offers an easier version. Tap "I'm not sore" and it learns.

What Hevy Pro and Kiron cost

Prices checked 2026-11-15, US App Store

The App Store lists two monthly prices for Hevy Pro, $2.99 and $3.99, and we couldn't confirm which one a new subscriber sees. Prices vary by region and offer.

On price, Hevy wins outright. Kiron's annual plan is {{kiron:price-annual}}, against Hevy Pro's $23.99. Kiron has no monthly plan: the weekly plan is {{kiron:price-weekly}}, which comes to {{kiron:price-weekly-yearly}} if you stay on it, so if you're paying for Kiron, the annual plan is the one to look at.

{{kiron:free-tier-sentence}} For anyone happy on Hevy's free plan, that's the biggest difference.

Who should pick Hevy

Pick Hevy if:

  • You already have routines you like and want to log them for free. A three- or four-day split fits in the free plan's four routines.
  • You want an app to write your lifting program. Trainer does that on Pro, for $23.99 a year, and moves the weights up for you.
  • Friends keep you going. Hevy has a feed, likes, comments and gym leaderboards. Kiron has none of that; you can share a workout by link or as a picture.
  • You log from your wrist. Hevy has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps. Kiron has no Watch app; it reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.
  • Your gym has no signal. Hevy's App Store listing says you can work out offline, with your data syncing across devices. Kiron needs a connection to open a workout.
  • You want a track record. Hevy's website says more than 18 million people use it. Kiron is new, with a small user base.

Weighing other logs? See how Strong compares, or, for an app that writes each workout for you, how Fitbod compares.

Bringing your Hevy workouts with you

If you do switch, your history can come with you. In Hevy, go to Profile, then Settings, then Export & Import Data, then Export Data, and choose Export Workouts. That gives you a CSV file. In Kiron, open Settings, tap Import from another app, and choose the file. Kiron shows how each exercise matched before anything is saved, and you can remove the import again later. It brings in finished workouts only; your Hevy routines stay behind, so you'd pick or paste a program in Kiron.

Two things to be fair about. Hevy's own importer takes Strong files only, so moving from Kiron back to Hevy isn't covered. And Kiron has no export at all, while Hevy exports your workouts and measurements. Keep your Hevy file either way. Our guide to exporting your workout history covers Hevy, Strong, Fitbod and others step by step.

Hevy FAQ: free, Pro and Trainer

Is Hevy free, and how many routines do you get?

Yes. Hevy's free plan has no ads and logs unlimited workouts, with up to 4 routines, 7 custom exercises and 3 months of data history. Pro removes those limits.

Is Hevy Pro worth it?

If you've outgrown 4 routines, want all your history, or want Trainer to build and progress a program, Pro gets you that for $23.99 a year or $74.99 once. If the free plan holds all your routines, you don't need it.

What is Hevy Trainer?

A Pro feature that builds a lifting program from your goal, experience, equipment and schedule, then suggests weight increases based on what you log. Hevy says it's algorithm-based rather than AI.

Can Hevy track running?

Hevy logs cardio with time and distance, and Trainer can add cardio to a program, but we didn't find running plans or GPS run tracking, so for structured running you'd pair it with a running app. Kiron puts running programs on the same calendar as lifting, though it doesn't show pace.

Can I import a ChatGPT workout plan into Hevy?

We didn't find a way to paste a plan into the Hevy app. You can type it in as routines, or type @hevy in ChatGPT to have ChatGPT build a plan and save it to your account. In Kiron, you paste the plan you already have, or photograph it, and it lands on your calendar. Our ChatGPT plan guide covers prompting for a good plan and checking it first.

If you want to try Kiron

If your plan came from ChatGPT, a coach or a book, or your week includes runs, paste the plan you already follow into Kiron and see it on a calendar. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you're happy logging your own routines, stay on Hevy's free plan. It does that job without costing anything.
